newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia on track for budget balance - Fahey.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia on track for budget balance - Fahey.

text.p: Australian Finance Minister John Fahey said on Sunday the government was still on track for a balanced underlying budget for the 1998/99 (June 30) fiscal year despite setbacks to its deficit cutting programme in the Senate.
Fahey said in a television interview that the rejection by the Senate of some budget proposals had resulted in a slippage of about A$750 million in the deficit cutting programme.
"There is still about another billion dollars that's there that we have asked the Senate to deliver to us," Fahey said.

"They should heed the warning from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry and deliver those savings because it is important to the nation's future that we get that fiscal consolidation, that our strategy remains in place," he said.
Fahey said the government would continue to work towards a balanced budget within the term of the current parliament.
"We're still on target to do that and we will still continue to apply the pressure as necessary to achieve that," he said on the Channel Seven "Face to Face" programme.
Fahey said the economy was roughly on track to deliver the two percent increase in employment and 8.25 percent unemployment rate that was forecast in the budget for 1996/97.
"We are broadly on target to achieve that," he said. The seasonally-adjusted jobless rate was 8.5 percent in November.
"The government recognises that one of the major issues that we have to address this year, and I suspect for many years, is the question of employment," Fahey said.
"We also acknowlege that as far as growth in the economy is concerned, the government has continued to acknowledge that it is patchy," he said. However, he said investment was strong.
He said further spending cuts would be examined. "...We will continue to look at savings, but they will be nowhere near the magnitude of what we had to achieve last year," Fahey said.
"We will find it through savings, not through higher taxes," he added.

The government has a solid majority in the lower House of Representatives, the seat of government power, but it needs the support of two independents to get legislation through the upper house, the Senate.
The underlying budget deficit -- which excludes asset sales -- was about A$10.3 billion in 1995/96.
"We forecast 14 percent (increase in capital expenditure) - it's about 18.6 percent on a recent survey there of business intentions," Fahey said.
